content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler Meat is a ready‑to‑eat product made from selected beef or chicken, thermally processed and finely minced to a tender texture. The product contains no added sugar, salt or artificial preservatives, making it suitable for children from 12 months old.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The product undergoes double heat treatment to ensure microbiological safety.
A small amount of natural herbs and spices, approved for infant nutrition, is used to enhance flavor.
Each serving provides about 20 % protein, essential for growth and development.
It is packaged in sealed portion‑size pouches that can be heated directly in a microwave.
Shelf life is 12 months when stored in a cool, dry place.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: High‑quality meat protein supports muscle growth and immune system development in toddlers.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Readily absorbable iron helps maintain normal blood formation and prevents anemia.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B12 and B6 contribute to nervous system function and energy metabolism.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: No added salt promotes healthy taste preferences in early childhood.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Fine texture and lack of tough fibers make the product gentle on a toddler’s stomach.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some children may develop an allergic reaction to beef or chicken; discontinue use if symptoms appear.

items.title: Overheating
items.content: Microwave heating can create hot spots; stir well before serving.

items.title: Storage after opening
items.content: Opened pouches should be refrigerated and consumed within 24 hours.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the product in a microwave (30‑40 seconds) or steam it, then stir to a smooth consistency. Serve as a standalone meal or mixed with vegetable puree.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep unopened packages in a cool, dry place at 5‑25 °C. After opening, refrigerate and use within one day.

cheese-sandwich-reduced-fat-cheese-on-wh.title: Cheese sandwich, reduced fat cheese, on white bread

content.title: About
content.content: A cheese sandwich with reduced‑fat cheese on white bread is a light snack consisting of two slices of soft white bread with a layer of low‑fat cheese in between. It is commonly served in cafeterias, cafés, and as part of school meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Reduced‑fat cheese contains less fat than regular cheese while retaining most of the protein and calcium.
White bread used in this sandwich is typically made without seeds or whole grains, giving it a soft, neutral flavor.
Cheese sandwiches are often included in school nutrition programs to provide children with essential nutrients.
The combination of dairy and bread offers a quick source of energy from carbohydrates and protein.
In some countries this sandwich is a traditional breakfast item for kindergartens.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Reduced‑fat cheese is a good source of calcium, important for bone and tooth health.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Cheese provides complete animal protein that supports tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with regular cheese, the reduced‑fat version contains less saturated fat, making it more suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Cheese supplies vitamin B12 and riboflavin, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Supports gut microbiota
items.content: Fermented dairy products can contribute to a healthy intestinal microbiome.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience bloating, gas, or diarrhea after eating cheese.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein or other milk proteins requires complete avoidance of the product.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some reduced‑fat cheeses are heavily salted, which may be unsuitable for hypertension.

items.title: High glycemic index of white bread
items.content: White bread can cause a rapid rise in blood glucose levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich can be eaten cold or lightly toasted. It is convenient to cut into small pieces for children’s meals or serve whole as a quick snack. Adding fresh vegetables such as tomato or cucumber can boost its nutritional value.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared sandwich in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C for no more than 24 hours. If bread and cheese are kept separately, they can be stored in airtight containers for up to 3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: A hamburger is a classic fast‑food item consisting of a medium beef patty (1702 g), a bun, lettuce, a tomato slice, cheese, pickles and sauce. It is quick to prepare and often served with fries and a drink.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first hamburger was served in the United States in the late 19th century.
There are more than 300 variations of toppings and sauces, from classic to exotic.
In Japan, rice‑bread buns are sometimes used instead of wheat buns.
The world’s largest hamburger weighed over 1 ton and was made in the USA in 2012.
In some countries the hamburger is considered a national dish.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: A medium patty (≈ 100 g) provides about 20 g of protein, essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef is rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Hamburgers supply vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The high calorie content offers a quick source of energy for active lifestyles.

items.title: Zinc content
items.content: Zinc from beef supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: High calories and saturated fat
items.content: One hamburger can contain 500‑800 kcal and a notable amount of saturated fat, which may be undesirable for weight management.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Sauces and processed buns often contain high levels of salt, potentially raising blood pressure.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Buns may contain gluten and dairy, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Nitrites in processed meat
items.content: Some pre‑made patties contain nitrites that can form potentially harmful compounds when cooked at high temperatures.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hamburgers are typically eaten by hand, holding the bottom bun. You can add extra vegetables, swap the sauce, or choose a whole‑grain bun for a healthier option.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked patties in the refrigerator for up to 2 days, and keep buns in a dry place for several days. Frozen patties retain quality for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: The “Multigrain” muffin is a soft baked good made from whole grains such as oats, barley, and rye. It has a light nutty note, moderate sweetness, and a dense yet tender crumb. Ideal for breakfast or a snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The recipe blends five different whole grains, boosting fiber content.
No artificial flavors or colorings are used in the muffins.
Each muffin provides about 30 % of the adult daily iron requirement.
The dough relies on natural gluten from whole grains, not on gluten substitutes.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole grains increase dietary fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates deliver sustained energy and prolonged satiety.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2 and B6 aid metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: The muffin supplies magnesium, iron and zinc, important for muscle and immune health.

items.title: Low added sugar
items.content: Sweetness comes from natural fruit purées, without refined sugar.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Contains wheat, barley and rye, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Despite nutritious ingredients, the muffin is relatively calorie‑dense; consume in moderation.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: A modest amount of salt is added; those monitoring sodium intake should take this into account.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the muffin as a standalone snack, split and spread with low‑fat cottage cheese, add to yogurt, or use as a base for an avocado toast.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days or refrigerate for up to 7 days. For longer storage, freeze in a freezer‑safe bag for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Papaya is a tropical fruit native to Southeast Asia, Central and South America. A ripe papaya has orange‑red flesh, a sweet aroma, and a soft, juicy texture. It is eaten fresh and used in salads, smoothies, desserts, and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Papaya belongs to the Caricaceae family and is a relative of mango and avocado.
Papaya seeds are edible but have a bitter taste and contain papain – an enzyme that aids digestion.
Warm, humid climates allow the fruit to mature in 6‑9 months.
Papaya is often used in cosmetics for its brightening and exfoliating properties.
In some cultures papaya symbolizes hospitality and abundance.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: One serving provides over 200 % of the daily vitamin C requirement, supporting immunity and protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains papain
items.content: Papain is a proteolytic enzyme that helps improve protein digestion and eases gastrointestinal discomfort.

items.title: Source of vitamin A and carotenoids
items.content: Beta‑carotene in papaya converts to vitamin A, essential for vision and skin health.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Potassium, magnesium, and dietary fiber in papaya help regulate blood pressure and cholesterol levels.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids and lycopene in papaya protect cells from free‑radical damage.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to papaya or its seeds, resulting in skin rashes or swelling.

items.title: Lactoferrin content
items.content: High amounts of lactoferrin can cause gastrointestinal upset in sensitive people.

items.title: Pregnancy caution
items.content: Excessive consumption of unripe papaya is thought to stimulate uterine contractions and should be avoided during pregnancy.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cut the flesh, discard the seeds, and eat the fruit fresh. It can be added to fruit salads, smoothies, yogurts, or used in sauces for fish and seafood. Dried seeds are sometimes used as a spice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ripe papaya in the refrigerator’s fruit drawer for 3‑5 days. Unripe fruits should be kept at room temperature until they mature, then moved to the fridge.

content.title: About
content.content: Pesto sauce is a classic Italian condiment made from fresh basil, olive oil, pine nuts, Parmesan cheese, and garlic. It has a bright aroma, rich flavor, and is used as a pasta dressing, spread on bread, or an accompaniment to meat and fish dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name pesto comes from the Italian verb “pestare,” meaning “to crush” in a mortar.
Traditional Genoese pesto is prepared in a marble mortar, which helps preserve the basil’s aroma.
Pine nuts in the original recipe can be substituted with walnuts or almonds without major flavor loss.
In the United States, pesto is often made with added spinach or parsley to reduce cost.
There are many pesto variations: arugula, sun‑dried tomato, pecan, and even avocado pesto.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Basil provides polyphenols and vitamin K, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Olive oil supplies monounsaturated fats that support heart health.

items.title: Source of vitamins A and C
items.content: Basil and garlic deliver vitamins A and C, important for immunity and vision.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Parmesan adds calcium and phosphorus, essential for strong bones.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Pine nuts and basil contribute modest amounts of fiber that aid digestion.

items.title: Nut allergy
items.content: Pine nuts can trigger allergic reactions in susceptible individuals.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Olive oil and nuts make the sauce calorie‑rich; portion control is advised.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Parmesan adds sodium, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Microbial risk
items.content: Fresh herbs can carry bacteria; keep the sauce refrigerated and consume within a week.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pesto pairs wonderfully with pasta, rice, couscous, as a marinade for chicken, fish or vegetables, and as a spread on bread, crackers, or sandwiches. It can be stirred into soups or used as a pizza sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store pesto in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5–7 days. For longer keeping, freeze in small portions; after thawing, stir as the oil may separate.

rice-brown-with-corn-fat-added.title: Brown Rice with Corn, Fat Added

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice with corn and added fat is a whole‑grain product that combines rice grains, whole corn kernels, and a small amount of vegetable oil to provide a balanced nutrient profile and a pleasant taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains the bran and germ, making it more nutritious than white rice.
Corn adds extra fiber and a subtle sweetness to the blend.
The added vegetable fat improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins and increases satiety.
This mix is often used in sports nutrition and child nutrition for higher energy density.
When stored properly, the product keeps its corn aroma for several months.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Both brown rice and corn provide dietary fiber that supports digestive health.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: The blend offers slow‑releasing energy, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Added vegetable oil (e.g., sunflower oil) supplies essential fatty acids.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The product contains thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which are important for carbohydrate metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It provides magnesium, phosphorus and iron, which are vital for bone health and blood formation.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Added fat increases the energy density, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Brown rice contains phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption when consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook the blend like regular rice (water‑to‑grain ratio 2:1), use it in salads, soups, casseroles, or as a side dish for meat. Rinse the rice before cooking to remove excess starch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct light. For long‑term storage, keep refrigerated to prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Soup‑tortilla is a ready‑to‑eat kit that includes a flavorful broth and a soft corn or wheat tortilla. The product is designed for quick preparation of a complete lunch or dinner, combining nutritious ingredients with convenience.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tortilla originates from Mexican cuisine and has been used for over 3,000 years.
Soup‑tortilla often contains spices such as cumin, paprika, and chili that give it a distinctive aroma.
Corn tortillas are gluten‑free, while wheat tortillas are softer and more pliable.
The ready‑made kit allows you to prepare the dish in 5‑7 minutes while retaining home‑cooked flavor.
Some versions include dried fruit or legumes to boost protein and fiber content.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The soup components (meat, vegetables, spices) are rich in vitamins B1, B2 and B6, which support metabolic processes.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain tortillas supply fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many ready meals, soup‑tortilla typically contains a modest amount of added fats.

items.title: Enriched with minerals
items.content: The kit often contains magnesium and iron, essential for muscle and blood health.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The broth supplies fluids and electrolytes, beneficial for an active lifestyle.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat tortillas contain gluten, which can be problematic for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared soups can be high in salt; individuals with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Thermal safety
items.content: Insufficiently heated soup may retain bacteria; bring it to a rolling boil before serving.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some kits may include food preservatives; those with sensitivities should choose preservative‑free options.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the broth to a boil, add the tortilla and let it soak for 1‑2 minutes. Optionally garnish with fresh vegetables, herbs, lime, or hot sauce. The tortilla can be torn into pieces and used as a dipper.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, consume within 3‑5 days and keep refrigerated.
